{{Short description|Statistical measure of a dendrogram's faithfulness to the data}}
In [[statistics]], and especially in [[biostatistics]], '''cophenetic correlation'''<ref>Sokal, R. R. and F. J. Rohlf. 1962. The comparison of dendrograms by objective methods.  Taxon, 11:33-40</ref> (more precisely, the '''cophenetic correlation coefficient''') is a measure of how faithfully a [[dendrogram]] preserves the pairwise distances between the original unmodeled data points. Although it has been most widely applied in the field of biostatistics (typically to assess cluster-based models of [[DNA]] sequences, or other [[Taxonomy (biology)|taxonomic]] models), it can also be used in other fields of inquiry where raw data tend to occur in clumps, or clusters.<ref>Dorthe B. Carr, Chris J. Young, Richard C. Aster, and Xioabing Zhang, [http://www.osti.gov/bridge/servlets/purl/9576-lcvvCD/webviewable/9576.pdf ''Cluster Analysis for CTBT Seismic Event Monitoring''] (a study prepared for the U.S. [[United States Department of Energy|Department of Energy]])</ref> This coefficient has also been proposed for use as a test for nested clusters.<ref>Rohlf, F. J. and David L. Fisher. 1968. Test for hierarchical structure in random data sets.  Systematic Zool., 17:407-412 ([http://life.bio.sunysb.edu/ee/rohlf/reprints/RohlfFisher_1968.pdf link])</ref>

==Calculating the cophenetic correlation coefficient==

Suppose that the original data {''X<sub>i</sub>''} have been modeled using a cluster method to produce a dendrogram {''T<sub>i</sub>''}; that is, a simplified model in which data that are "close" have been grouped into a hierarchical tree. Define the following distance measures.

* <math>x(i,j) = |X_i-X_j|</math>, the Euclidean distance between the ''i''th and ''j''th observations.
* <math>t(i,j)</math>, the dendrogrammatic distance between the model points <math>T_i</math> and <math>T_j</math>. This distance is the height of the node at which these two points are first joined together.

Then, letting <math>\bar{x}</math> be the average of the ''x''(''i'', ''j''), and letting <math>\bar{t}</math> be the average of the ''t''(''i'', ''j''), the cophenetic correlation coefficient ''c'' is given by<ref>[http://www.mathworks.com/access/helpdesk/help/toolbox/stats/index.html?/access/helpdesk/help/toolbox/stats/cophenet.html Mathworks statistics toolbox]</ref>

:<math>
c = \frac {\sum_{i<j} [x(i,j) - \bar{x}][t(i,j) - \bar{t}]}{\sqrt{\sum_{i<j}[x(i,j)-\bar{x}]^2 \sum_{i<j}[t(i,j)-\bar{t}]^2}}.
</math>

==Software implementation==
It is possible to calculate the cophenetic correlation in [[R (programming language)|R]] using the dendextend R package.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dendextend/vignettes/dendextend.html|title=Introduction to dendextend}}</ref>

In [[Python (programming language)|Python]], the [[SciPy]] package also has an implementation.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy-0.14.0/reference/generated/scipy.cluster.hierarchy.cophenet.html|title=scipy.cluster.hierarchy.cophenet — SciPy v0.14.0 Reference Guide|website=docs.scipy.org|access-date=2019-07-11}}</ref>

In [[MATLAB]], the Statistic and Machine Learning toolbox contains an implementation.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mathworks.com/help/stats/cophenet.html|title=Cophenetic correlation coefficient - MATLAB cophenet}}</ref>
